note.explanation: Transpiration from leaves creates a pulling force. This pull draws water up through the continuous water column in the xylem, from roots to leaves.
examples: Water evaporates from a leaf; more water then enters its mesophyll cells from the xylem.
When water moves up in the xylem of a leaf, it creates tension in the water column extending through the stem and roots.
note.checkAnswer: Transpiration of water from the leaf surfaces.
note.simple: Water leaving the leaves pulls more water upwards through the plant.
note.checkQuestion: What creates the pulling force in the leaves?
note.title: How water is pulled up a plant
steps: Water transpires from the leaf surfaces.
More water enters the mesophyll cells from the xylem.
The continuous water column extends from leaves through the stem to the roots.
Upward movement creates tension, pulling the water column upwards.
note.answer: Transpirational pull is the pulling force in leaves created by transpiration of water from their surfaces.

mcqs.stem: What directly creates the pulling force that moves water upwards in a plant?
rationales: Correct: transpiration from leaf surfaces creates the pulling force.
Incorrect: root hairs absorb water, but this is not the force pulling the water column upwards.
Incorrect: food transport in phloem is not the cause of water pull in xylem.
Incorrect: storing minerals does not create the pulling force.

mcqs.stem: In which tissue does the continuous water column extend from roots to leaves?
rationales: Correct: the water column is inside xylem vessels.
Incorrect: phloem transports food, not the water column described here.
Incorrect: root hairs absorb water but do not form the continuous column through the plant.
Incorrect: stomata are openings involved in transpiration, not the vessels carrying the column.

mcqs.stem: Which force helps create the continuous water column in xylem?
rationales: Correct: attraction among water molecules is one of the reasons for the continuous column.
Incorrect: repulsion would not help maintain a connected water column.
Incorrect: leaf width is not one of the stated reasons.
Incorrect: phloem food movement is unrelated to the water column.

options: Water molecules adhering to xylem walls
mcqs.stem: What does adhesion contribute to water transport in xylem?
rationales: Correct: water molecules adhere to the walls of xylem vessels.
Incorrect: repulsion from the walls is the opposite of adhesion.
Incorrect: xylem walls do not produce food as part of this mechanism.
Incorrect: root hairs do not close the xylem to create adhesion.

options: A tension in the whole water column
A break in the water column
mcqs.stem: What happens when one water molecule moves up through the xylem of a leaf?
rationales: Correct: its movement produces tension on the entire water column.
Incorrect: the described effect is tension, not a break in the column.
Incorrect: the result described is that the column is pulled upwards.
Incorrect: movement of a water molecule does not produce food in roots.

mcqs.stem: Which parts are included in the continuous water column described in the section?
rationales: Correct: the column extends from leaves to stem and roots.
Incorrect: the column does not stop at the leaves.
Incorrect: the text includes roots as well as the stem.
Incorrect: the column extends upwards beyond the roots.

written.text: Describe the mechanism of transport of water and salt in plants.
written.finalAnswer: Transpiration from the leaf surfaces creates a pulling force called transpirational pull. Water enters the mesophyll cells from the xylem. A continuous water column extends through xylem from leaves to stem and roots. Attraction among water molecules, the narrow diameter of xylem vessels, and adhesion of water molecules to xylem walls help maintain this column. Upward movement of water creates tension on the column, pulling it upwards through the plant.

written.text: Why do plants transpire more on a windy day compared to a humid one?
written.finalAnswer: Wind removes moist air from around the leaf, allowing more water vapour to leave its surface. Humid air already contains much water vapour, so less water vapour leaves the leaf; therefore, transpiration is lower in humid conditions.

For a full explanation, name transpiration as the cause, describe the continuous xylem water column, and state that tension pulls it upwards.
Remember all three stated reasons for the continuous water column: attraction among water molecules, narrow xylem vessels, and adhesion to xylem walls.
In a process answer, write the events in order: transpiration, water entering mesophyll cells from xylem, tension in the column, and upward pull.

explain.title: Transpirational pull
explain.body: “Roots cannot push the absorbed water to the leaves of the plant. Instead, the leaves apply a pulling force on water present in roots. The pulling force in leaves is created by the transpiration of water from their surfaces. Therefore, it is called transpirational pull.”

explain.title: The continuous water column
explain.body: “Inside xylem vessels, there is a continuous water column. This water column extends from leaves to stem and to the roots.”

explain.title: What keeps the column continuous
explain.body: “The continuous water column is created due to three reasons: (i) the forces of attraction among water molecules, (ii) the narrow diameter of xylem vessels, and (iii) the force by which water molecules are adhered to the walls of xylem vessels.”

explain.title: How the column moves upwards
explain.body: “When one water molecule moves up by the xylem of the leaf, it produces a tension on the entire water column in the xylem of leaves, stem and root. As a result, the entire water column is pulled upwards.”

mistakes: Do not say roots push water to the leaves; the section says leaves apply the pulling force.
Do not confuse xylem, which carries the water column, with phloem, which transports food.
Do not leave out the three stated reasons that help create the continuous water column.
Do not say tension acts only in the leaf; it acts on the entire water column in leaves, stem, and root.
Do not confuse the cause of the pull with its result: transpiration creates the pull, and tension pulls the column upwards.
